article_content: Donovan Webster, a 55-year-old acclaimed journalist and author from Charlottesville, Virginia, was taken into custody without bond on Monday on charges of driving under the influence following a crash that killed 75-year-old Wayne Thomas White, police said. Authorities from the Albemarle County Police Department confirmed the incident occurred Thursday in Afton — just outside Charlottesville — and involved two vehicles and a tractor-trailer. Webster was driving one of the vehicles; however, further details about the crash remain undisclosed. Webster, a former senior editor for Outside magazine and contributor to The New Yorker and National Geographic, has authored several books, including 'Meeting the Family: One Man's Journey Through His Human Ancestry,' 'The Burma Road: The Epic Story of the China-Burma-India Theater in World War II,' and 'Aftermath: The Remnants of War,' a collection of essays on the lasting impact of war on civilians. His book 'Aftermath' won the prestigious Gelber Prize in 1997, one of the world’s top honors for international affairs literature. To research his works, Webster traveled extensively to locations including France, Russia, Vietnam, Kuwait, and a weapons testing site in Nevada. His journeys inspired two documentaries: 'Running the Sahara' (2007), narrated by Matt Damon, and 'Amazon Gold' (2012), narrated by Sissy Spacek and Herbie Hancock. He also served as an editor for the Virginia Quarterly Review and taught media studies at the University of Virginia. Webster’s family confirmed to The Daily Progress that he is the individual charged in the crash but declined to offer further comment. Wayne Thomas White, a lifelong farmer and longtime employee of Friendly Tire Service in Waynesboro, is survived by 10 children, 19 grandchildren, and 10 great-grandchildren. Attempts to reach his family and a listed phone number for White were unsuccessful. A court hearing is scheduled for October. Additional charges may be filed pending the outcome of the ongoing investigation.

article_content: By Zoe Szathmary. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said on Thursday that she has not yet decided whether to run for president in 2016, but that she has been mulling it over. Clinton made the remarks during a one-hour interview with PBS journalist Charlie Rose on his program, part of her 'Hard Choices' book tour. When asked by Rose if her agenda would be revealed only after she makes a decision, Clinton replied, 'Yes, yes. If I decide to run, I will have a very specific agenda about what I think we should be doing.' But right now, we have a big election — the 2014 midterms — that could determine control of the Senate. And I'm not going to jump the line and start talking about 2016 right now. Earlier in the interview, Clinton said, 'You have to run a very specific campaign that talks about the changes you want to make in order to tackle growth, which is the handmaiden of inequality.' When pressed for a reason she might not seek office, Clinton revealed the reason 'would be wholly personal.' 'You know, I'm about to have my first grandchild, which I'm thrilled about — I can't wait... I want to see what that feels like,' she said, adding that she enjoys her current life. 'I've seen [the presidency] up close for more than 20 years,' she told Rose, referencing both her husband’s presidency and that of George W. Bush. 'Hard choices aren't necessarily the same for everyone,' she added. 'For some people, running for president is the next step in their career — and it's not hard at all.' Clinton reflected on the historic nature of a potential campaign, citing her 2008 bid for the Democratic nomination against then-Senator Barack Obama. 'But I also know the job has only gotten harder.' She noted that the president fulfills both the roles of head of state and head of government, but that government has fallen behind in providing adequate support for the position. 'I just have to decide whether that's what I want to do at this point in my life,' she said. 'It's a very personal choice.' Regarding her relationship with former President Bill Clinton, she described it as 'a deep, profound connection — love, companionship, support, and intellectual rapport.' 'It's all of that rolled up into one,' Clinton said.

Hvis jeg beslutter mig for at kandidere, vil jeg have et meget specifikt program om, hvad jeg tror, vi bør gøre.' Men for øjeblikket har vi en stor valgkamp — midtvalget i 2014 — der kan bestemme kontrollen over Senatet. Og jeg vil ikke hoppe foran og begynde at tale om 2016 lige nu. 'Det er alt det sammenfoldet i ét,' sagde Clinton.

article_content: Bamako, Mali (CNN) — Mali's historic cultural center, Timbuktu, lacks electricity, water, and phone service after 'terrorists' sabotaged its infrastructure, according to Moussa Ag Assarid, a Paris-based spokesman for the ethnic Tuareg separatist group MNLA. Assarid said most militants fled Timbuktu for the desert following French airstrikes on Tuesday that targeted their headquarters — a facility originally built by former Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi. However, he warned that some militants remain in the city. Assarid's use of the term 'terrorists' underscores the shifting alliances in Mali’s escalating conflict. The MNLA was previously allied with Ansar Dine, one of the main Islamist factions seeking to seize control of Mali. But after ousting the Malian army from Timbuktu last year, Ansar Dine and al-Qaeda drove the MNLA out. General Carter Ham, head of U.S. Africa Command, spoke at Howard University in Washington on Thursday, stating his goal is to help a legitimate Malian government based in Bamako regain full control of the country. The U.S. has conducted seven cargo flights to Mali. 'The territorial integrity of Mali is non-negotiable. There is no room for a separatist state,' Ham said. 'But Mali has requested — and will need — assistance to establish governance in the north.' He added, 'Realistically, we all want to see al-Qaeda eliminated from northern Mali. But the most achievable outcome is containment and disruption — preventing them from holding territory as they do today.' 'This effort must be African-led, at Mali’s request — and that is already underway,' Ham emphasized. Yet recent allegations against Malian troops have raised alarms among human rights groups. According to the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), Malian soldiers have carried out summary executions while pushing back Islamist militants. The military offensive, backed by France and other international partners, has intensified over the past two weeks. Refugees describe horrific conditions under Islamist rule, but FIDH reports that Malian forces are committing similar atrocities. Victims include those accused of aiding jihadists, possessing weapons, lacking identification during patrols, or belonging to specific ethnic groups — particularly Tuaregs. FIDH confirmed at least 11 executions in Sevare, near the military camp, bus station, and hospital. Reliable sources indicate nearly 20 more burials in nearby wells. In Niono, two Tuareg men were killed. Homes of Tuareg families have been looted, and many are hiding or fleeing to avoid reprisals. Malian military officials declined to comment on the allegations. FIDH demands an independent investigation to assess abuses and prosecute perpetrators. 'These acts of revenge, amid deep community tensions, form an explosive cocktail,' said FIDH President Souhayr Belhassen. 'We fear the worst is yet to come.' The MNLA, heavily armed after fighting for Gaddafi, launched a coup against Mali’s government last year. Islamist extremists exploited the power vacuum, imposing strict Sharia law: banning music, smoking, alcohol, and TV, and destroying ancient tombs and shrines. Amnesty International also condemned abuses by Malian forces and allied militias, noting that some perpetrators operate with impunity. A 2012 Amnesty report accused the Malian army of indiscriminate bombings targeting civilians during Tuareg rebellions. Corinne Dufka, head of Human Rights Watch in West Africa, told CNN that education and training in international humanitarian law are critical. 'This must be a wake-up call — to the Malian army to investigate and punish abusers, and to international partners — France, the EU, African forces — to recognize the flaws in Mali’s security forces and provide urgent mentoring to prevent further abuses,' she said. CNN reporters have heard anecdotal accounts of abuse and widespread anti-Tuareg sentiment. Many Malians blame Tuaregs for the conflict. Tuareg refugees confirm fleeing violence, often with nothing left but their lives. France intervened after militants announced on January 10 that they had captured Konna, east of Diabaly, and were advancing toward Bamako — raising fears Mali could become a terrorist safe haven. FIDH is a global coalition of 164 human rights organizations with offices at the UN, EU, and ICC. Reporting from Mali: Ingrid Formanek. From Atlanta: Joseph Netto and Mark Morgenstein. From Washington: Barbara Starr. From London: Laura Smith-Spark.

Assarid sagde, at de fleste militanters flygtede fra Timbuktu til ørkenen efter franske luftangreb på tirsdag, der ramte deres hovedkvarter — en facilitet oprindeligt bygget af den tidligere libyske leder Moammar Gaddafi. Dog advarede han mod, at nogle militantere stadig er i byen. Assarids brug af ordet 'terrorister' understreger de skiftende alliancer i Malis stigende konflikt. Men efter at have dræbt den maliske hær fra Timbuktu sidste år, drev Ansar Dine og al-Qaida MNLA væk. Generalmajor Carter Ham, chef for U.S. Africacom, talte på Howard University i Washington torsdag og sagde, at hans mål er at hjælpe en legitim malisk regering baseret i hovedstaden Bamako med at genoprette fuld kontrol over landet. USA har gennemført syv godstransporter til Mali. 'Malis territorielle integritet er ikke-forhandlingsbar. Der er ingen plads til et separatistisk stat', sagde Ham. Men det mest opnåelige resultat er indkapsling og forstyrrelse — så al-Qaida ikke længere kan holde territorium som de gør i dag.' 'Denne indsats skal være afrikansk-ledet, på Mali's anmodning — og det er allerede i gang,' understregede Ham. Men nylige anklager mod maliske tropper har skabt bekymring blandt menneskerettighedsorganisationer. Ifølge International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) har maliske soldater udført sammentrængte henrettelser, mens de forsøgte at fordrive islamistiske militantere. Den militære offensiv, støttet af Frankrig og andre internationale allierede, har intensiveret de seneste to uger. Flygtninge beskriver horribile forhold under islamistisk herredømme, men FIDH rapporterer, at maliske styrker begår lignende forbrydelser. Ofrene inkluderer dem, der er anklaget for at hjælpe jihadister, eje våben, ikke have identifikation under patruljer, eller tilhøre bestemte etniske grupper — især tuareger. FIDH bekræftede mindst 11 henrettelser i Sevare, nær militærcampen, busstationen og hospitalet. Pålidelige kilder antyder næsten 20 flere begravninger i nærheden af brønde. I Niono blev to tuareg-mænd dræbt. Huse hos tuareg-familier er blevet plyndret, og mange gemmer sig eller flygter for at undgå hævn. Maliske militære embedsmænd nægtede at kommentere anklagerne. FIDH kræver en uafhængig undersøgelseskommission til at vurdere omfanget af disse overtrædelser og straffe gerningsmændene. 'Disse hævnaktioner, i kombination med de store spændinger mellem samfundene, danner en eksplosiv blanding,' sagde FIDHs præsident Souhayr Belhassen. 'Vi frygter, at det værste endnu er kommet.' MNLA, tungt bevæbnede efter at have kæmpet for Gaddafi, udførte et kup mod Malis regering sidste år. Islamistiske ekstremister udnyttede magttomhed, og indførte streng sharia-lovgivning: forbud mod musik, rygning, alkohol og tv, samt ødelæggelse af gamle graver og helligdomme. Amnesty International har også fordømt overtrædelser af maliske styrker og allierede milits, og bemærkede, at nogle gerningsmænd opererer med frihed. Et Amnesty-rapport fra 2012 anklagede den maliske hær for 'ubestemt' bombning af civile under tuareg-opstande. Corinne Dufka, leder af Human Rights Watch i Vesteafrika, fortalte CNN, at uddannelse og træning i international menneskerettighedslovgivning er kritisk. 'Dette skal være en vækkelsesrop — til den maliske hær til at undersøge og straffe skyldige, og til de internationale partnere — Frankrig, EU, de afrikanske styrker — til at anerkende svaghederne i Malis sikkerhedskræfter og give hurtig vejledning, så der ikke sker flere overtrædelser i fremtiden,' sagde hun. CNN-reportere har hørt anekdotiske beretninger om overtrædelser og bred anti-tuareg-sentiment. Mange maliske borgere skylder tuaregerne for konflikten. Tuareg-flygtninge bekræfter, at de måtte flygte vold, ofte uden andet end deres liv. Frankrig indgik i konflikten efter, at militantere annoncerede den 10. januar, at de havde taget Konna, øst for Diabaly, og var på vej mod Bamako — hvilket skabte frygt for, at Mali kunne blive et terroristisk sikkerhedshavn. article_content: Education Secretary Michael Gove has defended politicians who choose private schools for their children, urging the public not to criticize such decisions. Speaking to the Daily Telegraph, Gove argued that parents—especially those in public office—must prioritize their children’s best interests above political optics. His comments came amid scrutiny of Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg, who is considering enrolling his 11-year-old son, Antonio, in a private school despite his party’s traditional support for state education. Clegg and his wife, Miriam Gonzalez Durantez, have visited both elite state institutions like The London Oratory and expensive independent schools costing £30,000 annually. While Prime Minister David Cameron pledged to send his daughter to a state school, Clegg declined to make a similar commitment. Gove countered that many senior Labour figures, including Tony Blair, Harriet Harman, and Diane Abbott, have also chosen private education for their children. 'I would defend anybody who makes any decision about a child’s education in their interests,' Gove said. 'It’s terrible politics to drag children into partisan debates.' He emphasized that parental responsibility comes before political pressure, adding that fierce competition for places in top London state schools makes private options a practical reality for many families.

article_content: In Indianapolis, 18-year-old Linda Kelley died under horrific conditions—wearing only a diaper, her body ravaged by deep, life-threatening bedsores that exposed bone and internal organs. Her parents, John and Lavonne Kelley, have been charged with felony neglect after authorities determined that prolonged lack of medical care and extreme unsanitary living conditions directly led to her death on August 4. The home, described as overrun with insects, trash, and animal waste, had been inspected just six days earlier by social workers from the Department of Child Services (DCS) and Damar Services, who reported no visible signs of abuse. Yet, upon returning after her death, one worker found the house transformed: filled with dog feces, cigarette butts, soiled diapers, and swarming pests—including bugs inside the refrigerator. Teresa Carter, the DCS case worker assigned to Linda, admitted she had not checked Linda’s legs for sores during her final visit, assuming previous injuries had healed. She was managing nearly twice the legally permitted number of cases and later said she was emotionally overwhelmed. Although the Kelleys had a documented history of neglect dating back to 1997, a court-approved plan in early 2023 had led officials to close the case in July, believing conditions had improved. Damar Services’ president, Jim Dalton, stated his team had never witnessed such a dire environment and would have reported it immediately had they seen it. Meanwhile, Lavonne Kelley reportedly told police she noticed skin damage two days before Linda died but claimed her daughter refused to go to the hospital or allow turning. The Marion County coroner cited poor hygiene and untreated pressure wounds as the direct causes of death. Judge Marilyn Moores concluded that while no records were falsified, there was clear 'negligent oversight' by multiple parties—including the parents, the DCS, and service providers—who collectively failed Linda in her final weeks.

Hendes forældre, John og Lavonne Kelley, er anklaget for alvorlig vernegle, da myndighederne fastslog, at længerevarig mangel på medicinsk behandling og yderst utilstrækkelige levevilkår direkte førte til hendes død den 4. august. Huset, beskrevet som oversvømmet af insekter, affald og dyrisk affør, var blevet inspiceret blot seks dage tidligere af sociale arbejdere fra Department of Child Services (DCS) og Damar Services, som rapporterede ingen synlige tegn på mishandling. Men efter hendes død fandt en arbejder huset forvandlet: fyldt med hundesnav, cigaretter, beskidte voksnerlomper og sværmende skadedyr – herunder insekter i køleskabet. Hun havde haft næsten dobbelt så mange tilfælde som den lovlige grænse og sagde senere, at hun var emocionelt overvældet. Marion Countys patologiske afdeling oplyste, at dårlig hygiejne og ubehandlede tryksår var de direkte årsager til døden. article_content: Los Angeles, California — The contentious issue of illegal immigration took center stage in California’s gubernatorial race as Nicky Diaz Santillan, a former housekeeper for Republican nominee Meg Whitman, accused her employer of exploitation and abuse. Santillan, who worked for Whitman for nine years, claims she was fired in June 2009 after requesting help with her immigration status — a move her attorney, Gloria Allred, called politically motivated. The Whitman campaign responded by presenting immigration and IRS documents Santillan allegedly submitted in 2000, including a Social Security card and California driver’s license, asserting she misrepresented her legal status at the time of hire. Whitman stated she relied on the employment agency to verify documentation and terminated Santillan only after learning she was undocumented. Allred countered that Whitman received multiple letters from the Social Security Administration between 2002 and 2009 alerting her to a mismatched Social Security number — letters Santillan says she saw discarded in Whitman’s trash. Allred argued that Whitman ignored clear warnings and failed to ask about legal status during the hiring process. Santillan recounted emotional details: when she approached Whitman in June 2009 seeking assistance, Whitman allegedly laughed and later instructed her to sever all contact — telling her, 'You have never seen me and I have never seen you.' She also alleged denial of maternity leave, unpaid mileage, and threats to her job if she took medical time off. Whitman’s campaign called the allegations a politically timed smear, pointing to Allred’s history of supporting Democratic candidates and the timing — just 35 days before the election. Senior advisor Rob Stutzman dismissed the claims as an attempt to distract from Democratic nominee Jerry Brown’s controversial debate performance, calling it 'politics of personal destruction.' While Whitman opposes strict border laws like Arizona’s SB 1070 and California’s Proposition 187, she advocates harsh penalties for employers who hire undocumented workers — including fines and temporary license suspensions — positioning herself as enforcing accountability rather than targeting individuals.

article_content: By Emily Allen. PUBLISHED: 12:10 EST, 30 October 2012. | UPDATED: 19:13 EST, 30 October 2012. A senior columnist at the New York Times has questioned whether former BBC director general Mark Thompson is fit to lead America’s most prestigious newspaper following revelations about the Jimmy Savile sex abuse scandal. Thompson has denied any knowledge of a BBC cover-up and pledged to assume his new role in New York as scheduled on November 12. But in a column, Joe Nocera challenged Thompson’s account, writing: 'Thompson winds up appearing willfully ignorant—and it makes you wonder what kind of organization the BBC was when he was running it—and what kind of leader he was. It also makes you wonder what kind of chief executive he’d be at The Times.' The critique comes after reports that Thompson’s office was alerted twice to claims that Savile, a late BBC presenter, sexually abused children on BBC premises—in May and again in September. On both occasions, a spokesperson for Thompson claimed the allegations were never escalated to him. Nocera noted that Thompson initially said he never heard rumors about Savile and only learned of the canceled 'Newsnight' investigation after it was shelved. 'Here is where it gets a little less plausible,' Nocera wrote. 'Thompson now says that at a cocktail party last December, a BBC reporter told him, “You must be worried about the 'Newsnight’ investigation into Jimmy Savile.” Soon after, Thompson asked his staff about the investigation and was told it had been killed—for journalistic reasons. He claims to have inquired no further—not even to ask what the investigation was about.' 'A few months later, the British press revealed that the BBC had, as The Daily Mail put it, “shelved the Jimmy Savile sex abuse investigation to protect its own reputation.”' 'Given the seriousness of sexual abuse allegations—look at what happened at Penn State—you would think Thompson and his team would have moved swiftly to investigate. But they did nothing.' Thompson, 55, maintains he has the full backing of his new employers. 'I do not believe there is anything I’ve done in relation to this matter that should in any way impinge on my ability to fully discharge the responsibilities I’ll have at the New York Times,' he said in a recent interview. Nocera, however, suggests that New York Times chairman and publisher Arthur Sulzberger is in a difficult position. 'He believes strongly that he’s got the executive he needs to lead The Times back to profitability,' Nocera wrote. 'Although he declined to be interviewed for this column, he appears to have accepted Thompson’s insistence that he knew nothing about the explosive allegations that surfaced just 50 days after accepting the Times job. Sulzberger is backing his man unreservedly.' 'For the sake of Times employees—and, more importantly, readers who want to see a vibrant New York Times Company—let’s hope his faith in Thompson is warranted. Otherwise, the BBC won’t be the only organization being asked tough questions about its judgment.'

article_content: In early August 2021, actor John Cena attended the premiere of 'The Suicide Squad' in Los Angeles — but months later, he became unexpectedly central to a very different Hollywood story. Warner Bros. had planned to delete the completed film 'Coyote vs. Acme,' a James Gunn-produced comedy starring Cena, solely to claim a $30 million tax deduction. The announcement triggered widespread public anger, particularly because the movie had already been fully shot, edited, and received glowing feedback from early viewers. Unlike past incidents — such as the shelving of 'Batgirl,' which WB claimed was due to poor quality — critics and audiences alike praised 'Coyote vs. Acme,' making the studio’s original rationale seem financially motivated rather than artistic. Facing mounting pressure, especially amid growing industry scrutiny following the SAG-AFTRA strike, Warner Bros. reversed course. Now, the film will be offered to other distributors, potentially for streaming or theatrical release. While the studio initially said it had 'made the difficult decision not to move forward,' the phrase now appears misleading; 'not moving forward' meant destroying a finished product, not pausing development. The episode echoes similar moves by Disney+, which canceled completed shows like 'Spiderwick Chronicles' for budget reasons. Some observers believe the controversy may have inadvertently boosted the film’s market value, turning a corporate misstep into a marketing opportunity. Whether this signals a lasting shift in studio behavior remains to be seen — but one thing is clear: audiences won’t stay silent when their favorite projects are erased for accounting purposes.

article_content: Standing in Ploshtad Sveta Nedelya—the bustling square at the heart of Sofia—I’m momentarily disoriented, unsure what century I’m in. Behind me, Sveta Nedelya Cathedral rises as a dark, imposing relic of the 19th century, standing just steps from the 16th-century Banya Bashi Mosque. Ahead, the austere facade of the TZUM department store looms as a stark echo of communist-era architecture, while beneath my feet, the glass-covered ruins of ancient Serdica whisper of Rome’s long shadow. Only when the nearby metro station erupts with a rush of commuters does the 21st century feel undeniably real. The majestic Aleksandar Nevski Cathedral dominates Sofia’s skyline—a cathedral so grand it belongs on a million postcards. Built between 1878 and 1912 during Bulgaria’s close ties to Tsarist Russia, its golden domes and intricate mosaics evoke Moscow more than the Balkans. Inside, the scent of incense lingers as light filters through stained glass, illuminating vast, reverent spaces. Nearby, the modest St Sophia Church, unchanged since the 6th century, holds medieval frescoes where saints watch silently over worshippers. Sofia is one of Europe’s most historically dense capitals—and yet, it remains one of its least visited. Few cities wear their past so openly: Greek foundations, Roman roads, Ottoman minarets, Soviet concrete, and modern cafés all occupy the same streets. From the National Art Gallery, housed in a former royal palace, to the sprawling National Museum of History in Boyana—where the glittering Panagyurishte Treasure and Cold War relics tell a sweeping story—Sofia rewards those who dig deeper. But Sofia isn’t frozen in time. At Tsentralni Halite, the 1911 market hall buzzes with organic oils, artisan cheeses, and bottles of Bulgaria’s surprisingly refined wines. Vitosha Boulevard, mostly pedestrianized, hums with families, coffee drinkers, and evening revelers. Beyond its tree-lined stretch, Vitosha Mountain rises, dusted with snow—home to ski resorts just half an hour away. Evening reveals Sofia’s contemporary soul: Dada Cultural Bar, with its curated cocktails and hushed sophistication, feels as at home in Berlin as it does here. At Moskovska 15, a softly lit gem of fine dining, beef with herb-and-potato purée pairs perfectly with a velvety Bulgarian merlot. Why isn’t this city on everyone’s list? Perhaps because it doesn’t shout—but if you listen closely, it sings. With direct three-hour flights from London Heathrow and affordable stays like the Grand Hotel Sofia, there’s never been a better time to discover one of Europe’s best-kept secrets.

Bygget mellem 1878 og 1912 under Bulgariets tætte bånd til tsaristisk Rusland, udløser dens gyldne kupler og indviklede mosaikeer assocationer til Moskva snarere end Balkan. Sofia er en af Europas mest historisk tæt bebyggede hovedstæder – og alligevel en af de mindst besøgte. Få byer bærer deres fortid så åbenligt: græske grundlag, romerske veje, ottomanske minareter, sovjetisk beton og moderne caféer lever alle sammen på samme gader. Fra National Kunstgalleri, beliggende i et tidligere kongepalæ, til det udstrakte Nationale Historiemuseum i Boyana – hvor det glimrende Panagyurishte-skat og kolde krigsrelikvier fortæller en omfattende historie – belønner Sofia dem, der dykker dybere. article_content: The rise of breakfast biscuits may have seemed like a naughty start to the day for some, but the latest food trend to hit the UK delivers an even sweeter punch at the crack of dawn: breakfast gelato. Inspired by Italy’s beloved dessert, the UK’s first-ever breakfast gelato menu has launched at Comboco in Soho, London. With an array of quirky flavors, it challenges even the sweetest tooth. Options include cereal milk gelato—inspired by the sweet, starchy milk Americans often add to their breakfast bowls—and unusual combinations like pancakes and maple syrup, and toast with whipped butter. For those on a diet, frozen yogurt with granola offers a lighter alternative. And for post-party recovery, there’s the Bloody Mary gelato: a chilled tomato sorbet spiked with Tabasco and Worcestershire sauce. Coffee lovers can fuel their mornings with double espresso gelato. Other inventive offerings include avocado, pear, and gorgonzola; scrambled eggs; and opulent truffle oil and mushroom gelato. Traditional favorites like Bronte pistachio, Kentish strawberry, and Madagascan vanilla round out the menu. Dairy-based gelato typically contains 16–24% sugar, with 100g delivering around 216 calories. While not recommended for daily consumption, Comboco suggests the cold stimulus may aid hangover recovery by increasing blood flow to the brain. Founded by former City worker Ashish Saggar—who previously created special flavors for Pacha’s launch for River Island—the team describes the menu as ‘a bit of fun to cheer up the capital after this dull start to summer.’ They emphasize that all flavors use organic milk but advise city dwellers to enjoy this indulgence only on special occasions.

article_content: When the clock strikes midnight on New Year’s Eve, millions reach for a bottle of champagne to celebrate. But if you’re going to toast with it, why not know a thing or two about what’s in your glass? You’ll sound smart — not just buzzed. Here’s what you need to know. True champagne can only come from the Champagne region in northeastern France. Sparkling wine from elsewhere? It’s just sparkling wine. France has fiercely defended this designation since the 1891 Treaty of Madrid — a right later reinforced by the Treaty of Versailles and now protected by the European Union. The only exception? A small number of U.S. producers who legally used the term ‘champagne’ before 2006 and are grandfathered in. Real champagne is made using the Méthode Champenoise. Grapes are pressed and fermented like regular wine, then bottled with a precise mix of yeast and sugar. This triggers a second fermentation inside the bottle — the process that creates those signature bubbles. After aging on the dead yeast cells — called lees — for at least 15 months, bottles are gradually inverted to collect the sediment. The lees are then removed, a small amount of sugar (dosage) is added to adjust sweetness, and the bottle is sealed with a cork. What makes Champagne’s wine so special? Its cool northern climate preserves natural acidity in grapes like Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Pinot Meunier — ideal for sparkling wine. The region’s ancient, chalky soil, formed by prehistoric earthquakes, provides excellent drainage and mineral richness. You don’t need to break the bank for Dom Pérignon. High-quality sparkling wines come from Italy (Prosecco), Spain (Cava), California, Australia, and beyond — often at a fraction of the price and with incredible flavor. Contrary to legend, Dom Pérignon didn’t invent champagne. He was a Benedictine monk in the late 1600s who revolutionized production by improving bottle strength and securing corks with wire mesh — reducing dangerous explosions caused by unpredictable fermentation. ‘Brut’ and ‘extra brut’ indicate sweetness levels. Extra brut has less than 6 grams of sugar per liter; brut contains under 15 grams. Drier styles dominate today’s market. The tradition of spraying champagne began in 1967. After winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans, drivers Dan Gurney and A.J. Foyt shook a bottle and sprayed their team and Ford executives on the podium. The crowd erupted — and a new celebration ritual was born. Then there’s sabrage — opening champagne with a sword. Post-French Revolution, Napoleon’s cavalry sought a more dramatic way to uncork bottles. They’d strike the neck with a saber, cleanly separating the top and releasing the cork in a spectacular burst. Today, ceremonial sabers are sold for this very purpose. But beware: flying cork and shattered glass? It’s not just risky — it’s potentially dangerous. Leave it to the pros.

article_content: A photo provided by the Uttarakhand State Disaster Response Force shows rescuers working inside a collapsed road tunnel where 40 workers were trapped by a landslide in northern India on Sunday. On Monday, rescuers continued digging through debris to reach the workers at a construction site in Uttarakhand, a mountainous state known for its Hindu pilgrimage sites. Police officer Prashant Kumar confirmed all 40 workers are alive and have been supplied with oxygen and water. Rescuers have established communication with those trapped. The collapse occurred along the Chardham all-weather road project—a flagship federal initiative linking key Hindu pilgrimage destinations. Rajesh Pawar, project manager at Navyug Construction Company, confirmed the number of trapped workers. Rescue efforts began Sunday, with authorities pumping oxygen into the tunnel through a pipe. According to Kumar, rescuers have advanced 15 meters into the 50-meter blocked section, leaving 35 meters to clear. More than 150 personnel are using drills and excavators to remove rubble around the clock. The collapsed segment lies roughly 200 meters from the tunnel entrance, officials told the Press Trust of India. This incident echoes past instability in the region: in January, Uttarakhand authorities evacuated hundreds after land subsidence caused a temple collapse and damaged over 600 homes in Joshimath.

article_content: By Dan Bloom. Gentle Jess, a 12-year-old Springer Spaniel, is spending Easter on her family’s Devon farm by caring for a brood of newly hatched chicks. She proudly carries the fluffy yellow chicks in an egg basket around the yard, keeping them safe. When one wanders off, Jess gently offers her paw as a resting spot. Her owner, Louise Moorhouse, who raises sheep on the 180-acre farm near Exeter, isn’t surprised. Jess has helped care for newborn lambs since she was a puppy, even assisting with bottle-feeding. Jess is one ray of sunshine this Easter weekend — as forecasters predict patchy, unsettled weather across much of the UK. Southern England is expected to be cloudy and cool, with rain moving in. Northern England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland will remain mostly dry. Yesterday, millions took advantage of warm bank holiday weather, flocking to beaches, rivers, and parks, and clearing supermarket shelves of barbecues and charcoal. Sainsbury’s predicted sales of barbecue products would be five times higher than usual, with estimates of 375,000 burger packs, 7,000 disposable barbecues, and 56 tonnes of charcoal sold on Easter Sunday alone. Sales of coleslaw, dips, and sausage rolls also rose sharply. Tesco reported a 338% increase in charcoal and wood sales compared to last year, and a ninefold surge in garden products. Asda expects to sell one million legs of lamb, 200,000 sides of beef, and 200,000 pork joints. But the sunshine won’t last. Heavy showers and thunderstorms are expected to spread across southeast England by morning, reaching central and southwestern England and Wales by afternoon. The weather will be particularly harsh for those planning outdoor Easter Sunday meals. Scotland, northern England, and Northern Ireland are forecast to enjoy the best conditions over the long weekend, with dry and fine weather expected through Sunday and Monday. MeteoGroup forecaster Chris Burton said: 'It will stay dry and fine across Scotland, Northern Ireland, and northern England. But conditions will deteriorate across southern areas, with heavy showers and possible thunderstorms moving northward.' The Met Office predicts temperatures will peak at 15°C in northwest England and northern Scotland. An estimated 3.4 million people are taking holidays within the UK this Easter, with another 1.6 million traveling abroad. Additionally, 6.5 million Britons are expected to take day trips. Meanwhile, in Dudley, West Midlands, a 44-year-old man was arrested at 2:40 a.m. after driving into a police patrol vehicle, injuring two officers. No serious injuries were reported. Chief Inspector Jack Hadley of West Midlands Police urged: 'Think carefully before getting behind the wheel this weekend — there is absolutely no excuse for drunk driving.' In other scenes of celebration, crowds enjoyed the sunshine at the Whitby Scooter Rally, Virginia Water in Surrey, and the River Cam in Cambridge — moments now contrasted by the approaching rain.

article_content: LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — President Obama blended humor with serious policy discussion during a historic appearance on 'The Tonight Show with Jay Leno' on Thursday. While presidential candidates have appeared on comedy shows since Richard Nixon’s 1968 segment on 'Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In,' Obama became the first sitting U.S. president to perform before a late-night talk show studio audience. During the taping, Obama complimented guitarist Kevin Eubanks on his suit and joked about the Secret Service and 'American Idol' host Simon Cowell. He also poked fun at his own bowling skills, recalling a score of 129 at the White House bowling alley and quipping, 'It's like the Special Olympics or something.' Deputy Press Secretary Bill Burton quickly clarified that the president’s remark was never meant to mock the Special Olympics. 'The president made an offhand comment about his own bowling, in no way intended to disparage the Special Olympics,' Burton said. 'He views the Special Olympics as a wonderful program that empowers people with disabilities worldwide.' Obama then shifted to pressing economic issues, including the AIG bailout and the controversial $165 million in bonuses paid to executives after the company received $173 billion in federal aid. 'The problem with AIG was that it was so deeply entangled with banks and institutions that allowing it to collapse could have triggered a systemic financial meltdown,' Obama explained. 'Intervening was the right decision.' He acknowledged responsibility for the bonuses, stating, 'I’ll take responsibility.' He added, 'We need to return to values where people understand enough is enough — where personal accountability and shared sacrifice are part of the culture.' Obama voiced strong support for Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner: 'I think he’s doing an outstanding job. We’ve got a big mess, but it’s going to be fixed.' He also reflected on the isolation of the presidency, noting how Secret Service agents wouldn’t let him walk 750 yards from Air Force One to the Costa Mesa fairgrounds — though he joked that flying aboard Air Force One is 'pretty cool,' especially because 'they give you the jacket with the presidential seal on it.' Leno’s most pointed question came when he asked if opponents intentionally lose basketball games against the president. Obama replied, 'I don’t see why they’d throw the game — unless those Secret Service guys with guns are watching.' Media analyst Howard Kurtz of the Washington Post and CNN’s 'Reliable Sources' warned of political risk: 'He must be cautious. If he seems too jovial while millions struggle economically, it could create a jarring disconnect.'

article_content: Islamabad, Pakistan (CNN) — An eighth-grade girl has been awarded Pakistan’s first National Peace Prize for her online diary documenting the Taliban’s ban on girls’ education. Malala Yousafzai, a 14-year-old resident of Swat Valley in northwest Pakistan — one of the country’s most conservative regions — wrote openly about her struggle against extremist militants who used fear and intimidation to prevent girls from attending school. Using the internet, she shared her daily reality with the outside world, risking severe punishment. 'I was scared of being beheaded by the Taliban because of my passion for education,' Yousafzai told CNN. 'During their rule, they would storm into our homes to check if we were studying or watching television.' She often hid her books under her bed, fearing raids. On Thursday, Prime Minister Yusuf Raza Gilani announced the award, which includes a 500,000-rupee ($5,780) cash prize. His office stated that the Cabinet has been directed to award the National Peace Prize annually to a child under 18 who makes a significant contribution to peace and education in Pakistan. Malala was also among five global nominees for the 2011 International Children’s Peace Prize, selected from 42 countries. The award, presented by Nobel laureate Mairead Maguire on Monday, went to 17-year-old Michaela Mycroft of South Africa for her advocacy for children with disabilities. Although Malala did not win the international prize, she affirmed her commitment: 'I will continue to fight for girls’ education and work toward a society where girls can learn freely.' She also expressed ambitions for the future: 'I want to be a political leader — this country needs honest and true leaders.' Swat Valley remained under Taliban control until 2009, when a military operation displaced thousands and restored government authority. Journalist Shaan Khan contributed to this report.

article_content: By Hugo Gye. A mother from Essex has been told she is not entitled to a British passport because her father is not named on her birth certificate. Christine North has lived in Britain since she was seven and is the daughter of a British Army soldier who met her mother while stationed in Germany. She is married to an Englishman, has served on two juries, and has voted in every election since turning 18. Yet, the 32-year-old is not officially recognized as a UK citizen because she cannot prove her father was British. Her mother, Beate Toepke, met Christine’s father, Alan Griffiths — a Mancunian soldier — at a British Army base in Dortmund, Germany. Due to their turbulent relationship, Ms. Toepke did not list Mr. Griffiths as Christine’s father on her birth certificate. She later married another British soldier, Kevin Johnson, and moved to the UK when Christine was seven. Mrs. North, who lives in Clacton, Essex, says she considers herself entirely British. When she first applied for a passport, she was stunned to learn she was ineligible. 'I was told I might not be a British citizen,' she said. 'I was dumbfounded. I was passed from passport information to border control and then to immigration. At one point, they told me I might be deported. I was scared they would take me away from my family one day.' For a time, she claimed disability benefits due to a long-term health condition — and was warned she might have to repay them all. 'In the space of a few hours on the phone, my world was turned upside down.' She later realized the issue stemmed from her father’s absence on her birth certificate — despite his payment of child support during her upbringing. 'He wasn’t listed because of the difficulties between him and my mum,' she said. 'But as far as I’m concerned, I’m English. I was raised and educated that way, and I’ve lived here since childhood.' Christine has approached German authorities to obtain a German passport for international travel but insists the law must change to recognize her British identity. Under current rules, she would need to pass a 'Life in the UK' test and meet residency requirements to naturalize — despite being married to a British citizen and having lived in the UK most of her life. 'It’s absolutely ridiculous that I’m being asked to take a citizenship test about Shakespeare and British monarchs,' she said. 'I’m being punished because my biological father wasn’t involved. I spoke to officials at the German Embassy, and they just laughed: “Why would you belong to us?” — and they’re right. I am British.' 'I just want my passport, and I won’t stop until I get one. Right now, I’m stateless. I don’t have a home.' Her local MP, Conservative backbencher Douglas Carswell, called her situation 'bizarre' and pledged to lobby the government. 'Christine has fallen through a ludicrous loophole in the law,' he said. 'She is as British as anyone here — a Clacton woman through and through. If this system offers no human discretion, then it is profoundly broken. Anyone who hears these facts knows how absurd this is — yet officials just shrug. It’s quite insane.'

Men den 32-årige er ikke officielt anerkendt som britisk statsborger, fordi hun ikke kan bevise, at hendes far var britisk. Hendes mor, Beate Toepke, mødte Christines far, Alan Griffiths – en mand fra Manchester – på en britisk hærbas i Dortmund, Tyskland. På grund af deres urolige forhold listede hun ikke hr. Griffiths som Christines far på hendes fødselsattest. Senere giftede hun sig med en anden britisk soldat, Kevin Johnson, og flyttede til Storbritannien, da hendes datter var syv. Mrs. North, som bor i Clacton, Essex, siger, at hun anses for helt britisk. Da hun første gang søgte om et pas, var hun chokeret over at lære, at hun ikke var berettiget. I en periode modtog hun sygedagpenge på grund af en langvarig sundhedssituation – og blev advaret om, at hun måske skulle tilbagebetale dem alle. Senere indså hun, at problemet var, at hendes far ikke stod på fødselsattesten – trods at han havde betalt børneunderstøttelse under hendes opvækst. Jeg er britisk.' 'Jeg vil bare have mit pas, og jeg vil ikke holde op, før jeg får et. For øjeblikket er jeg statsløs. Jeg har ingen hjem.' Hendes lokale folketingsmedlem, konservativ bagbænksmedlem Douglas Carswell, kaldte hendes tilstand 'bizarre' og lovede at presse regeringen. 'Christine er faldet igennem en latterlig huller i loven,' sagde han. 'Hun er lige så britisk som enhver her – en rigtig Clacton-kvinde. Hvis dette system ikke giver plads til menneskelig fleksibilitet, så er det dybt forkert. Enhver, der hører disse fakta, ved, hvor absurdt det er – men når man peger på det for embedsmænd, så ryster de bare på hovedet. Det er helt vildt.'

article_content: Meeting someone new can be daunting — but for many young women in China, the challenge is compounded by intense pressure from parents to find a suitable partner. To avoid awkward family interrogations, some resort to hiring fake boyfriends for the duration of their visits. Now, the e-commerce platform Taobao has introduced a rent-a-boyfriend service, allowing men to advertise themselves as temporary companions — complete with detailed price lists. According to China’s People’s Daily, these arrangements typically require a minimum three-day commitment. Services include dinner (50 yuan, about £5), shopping trips (30 yuan, roughly £3), and an hourly rate of 30 yuan. Additional offerings: watching a movie (double the fee for thrillers), a 50-yuan kiss on the lips, and complimentary hand-holding or a farewell kiss on the cheek or forehead. Matthew Fang, a 27-year-old from Chongqing, started offering this service after graduating university. 'It’s not bad work,' he says, 'especially during Lunar New Year, when everyone’s watching.' Before each engagement, clients and fake boyfriends usually meet to align on backstories, exchange photos, and rehearse interactions. While most treat it as a straightforward job, some admit emotional strain. 'It depends how you see it,' says Xu Li, 26, from Yancheng. 'If you treat it as business, it’s easier.' Interestingly, this isn’t unique to China. The New York Observer recently reported on a growing trend among affluent Americans who hire paid friends — not for romance, but for companionship. One anonymous source described the experience as 'like being a pet monkey' — glamorous at times, demeaning at others. 'You put your ego away a long time ago,' he added.

article_content: NEW DELHI: Despite being overlooked by selectors for the T20I series against Australia, leg-spinner Yuzvendra Chahal turned his disappointment into motivation during Haryana’s Vijay Hazare Trophy campaign in Ahmedabad. In a stellar performance, the 33-year-old took a remarkable six-wicket haul (10-2-26-6), helping Haryana restrict Uttarakhand to 207 in their Group C match. Chahal’s exceptional bowling also marked his achievement of reaching 200 List A wickets — a milestone that could reignite his case for national selection. For Uttarakhand, wicketkeeper-batsman Aditya Tare scored 67, while opener Kunal Chandela added 47. However, Chahal dismantled the rest of the batting order. In reply, Haryana’s openers Yuvraj Singh (68) and Ankit Kumar (49) laid a solid foundation, and captain Ashok Maneria’s unbeaten 44 sealed a comfortable six-wicket victory. In Group A, Kerala edged out Saurashtra by three wickets in a tense contest at the Alur-KSCA Oval in Bengaluru. Saurashtra, reeling at 65 for 7, were rescued by Vishvarajsinh Jadeja’s resilient 98 off 121 balls. Despite cloudy conditions and a fresh pitch, they posted 185. Kerala’s debutant Akhin shone with the ball, claiming 4 for 39 to break the top order. Chasing 186, Kerala slumped to 61 for 4 in the 17th over, but Abdul Bazith’s composed 60 off 76 balls and Shreyas Gopal’s unbeaten 21 guided them home with 14 balls to spare. In Group A at Alur 2, Mumbai crushed Sikkim by seven wickets after pacer Tushar Deshpande took 3 for 19 to bowl them out for just 89 in 38.1 overs. Mumbai chased the target in just 12 overs, powered by Angkrish Raghuvanshi’s blistering 30 off 28 balls. In Group C at Motera 'A', Delhi bowled out Bihar for 149 thanks to a combined effort from veteran Ishant Sharma (3/30), Harshit Rana (4/17), and leg-spinner Suyash Sharma (3/19). Openers Yash Dhull (46*), Anuj Rawat (33), and Priyansh Arya (45) comfortably chased down the target in 22.1 overs. In Group C at Motera 'B', Karnataka posted their highest-ever List A total of 402 for 2, fueled by Mayank Agarwal’s 157 off 133 balls and Ravikumar Samarth’s 123 off 120 balls, supported by Devdutt Padikkal’s rapid 71 off 35 balls. Pacer Vysakh Vijayakumar then claimed 4 for 57 as Karnataka bowled out Jammu & Kashmir for 180, winning by 222 runs. In Group E at BKC, Mumbai, Bengal crushed Nagaland by nine wickets after pacers Saksham Chaudhary (3/23) and Akash Deep (2/24) restricted Nagaland to 139 in 47 overs. Captain Sudip Kumar Gharami (62* off 44 balls) and opener Abhimanyu Easwaran (57* off 63) guided Bengal to victory in just 18.5 overs.

article_content: The world's population has more than tripled since I was born in 1938. On Monday, the global population reached the milestone of 7 billion — up from 2.5 billion in 1950 — with nearly all growth occurring in the cities of less-developed countries. This means the challenges the world faced during my childhood are even more urgent for my grandchildren today. If fertility rates remain at projected levels, the world’s population is likely to reach 10.1 billion within the next 90 years. Conservative estimates suggest the population will surpass 8 billion in 2023, 9 billion by 2041, and 10 billion sometime after 2081. Consider this: by 2100, we could have nearly 50% more people on Earth than at the start of the century, all competing for the same finite resources — food, water, land, and attention. One of the most effective ways to ensure the 7 billionth child is born into a safe, healthy, and sustainable world is to prioritize what women want and need. Researchers at the Guttmacher Institute found that 215 million women worldwide desire the ability to time and space their pregnancies but lack access to effective contraception. Women want to give birth safely and provide for their children. According to the World Health Organization, complications from pregnancy and childbirth remain the leading cause of death among women of reproductive age in developing countries. In high-income nations, one in 4,300 women dies due to pregnancy-related causes. In sub-Saharan Africa, that rate is one in 31. In Afghanistan, one in eight women dies in childbirth. The tragic reality? One-third of these deaths could be prevented if women had access to voluntary family planning services. Universal access to voluntary family planning is a cost-effective, cross-cutting solution to achieving all the Millennium Development Goals. Beyond reducing maternal mortality, it helps young women avoid early pregnancy, enables more girls to stay in school longer, allows women to have fewer, healthier children, and breaks the intergenerational cycle of poverty. It also reduces HIV transmission, empowers women to engage in income-generating activities, and supports environmental sustainability. This is also a smart financial investment. International family planning delivers one of the highest returns on investment of any development intervention. Research from the Guttmacher Institute shows that providing quality reproductive health care and modern contraceptives to all women who want and need them reduces maternal and newborn care costs — yielding a net savings of $1.5 billion for every dollar spent. Despite its low cost and immense benefits, voluntary family planning has not consistently received adequate funding from world leaders. The current economic climate has compelled Congress to reassess spending priorities — and rightly so. But too often, the needs of women and children are the first to be cut. This year’s budget debates were no exception. Two of the most troubling and shortsighted cuts involve funding for international family planning and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). UNFPA is the UN agency dedicated to helping governments deliver comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care — including voluntary family planning — throughout women’s lives around the world. One of the wisest investments I ever made was my $1 billion donation to the United Nations, which helped establish the United Nations Foundation. The UN remains the only institution with the global reach and capacity to tackle today’s most pressing challenges. If we want to leave our children and grandchildren a safe and healthy planet, world leaders must support the UN’s critical work on voluntary family planning and reproductive health. The time to act is now. The investments we make today will define the world we hand to the next generation. To maintain its global leadership, the United States must prioritize smart, forward-looking investments that address both present and future responsibilities. The best way to do that is to listen to women — and fund international family planning. Our future depends on it. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Ted Turner.
translated_content: Verdens befolkning er mere end tredoblet siden jeg blev født i 1938. På mandag nåede verdens befolkning milepælen på 7 milliarder — op fra 2,5 milliarder i 1950 — med næsten hele væksten sket i byerne i mindre udviklede lande. Det betyder, at de udfordringer verden stod overfor under min barndom er endnu mere akutte for mine børnebørn i dag. Hvis frugtbarhedsraterne forbliver på de forventede niveauer, vil verdens befolkning sandsynligvis nå 10,1 milliarder inden for de næste 90 år. Konservative estimeringer antyder, at befolkningen vil overstige 8 milliarder i 2023, 9 milliarder i 2041 og 10 milliarder et tidspunkt efter 2081. Tænk på dette: i år 2100 kan vi have næsten 50 % flere mennesker på Jorden end ved begyndelsen af århundredet, alle konkurrerende om de samme begrænsede ressourcer — mad, vand, jord og opmærksomhed. En af de mest effektive måder at sikre, at den syvende milliards børn bliver født i en sikker, sund og bæredygtig verden, er at prioritere, hvad kvinder ønsker og har brug for. Forskere ved Guttmacher-instituttet fandt, at 215 millioner kvinder over hele verden ønsker at kunne planlægge og afstande deres graviditeter, men ikke har adgang til effektive former for prævention. Kvinder ønsker at føde sikkert og kunne forsørge deres børn. Ifølge Verdens Sundhedsorganisation er komplikationer fra graviditet og fødsel den førende årsag til død blandt kvinder i reproduktiv alder i udviklingslande. I rigeste lande dør én ud af 4.300 kvinder på grund af svangerskabsrelaterede årsager. I Sub-Saharisk Afrika er denne rate én ud af 31. I Afghanistan dør én ud af otte kvinder ved fødsel. Den tragiske virkelighed? En tredjedel af disse dødsfald kunne undgås, hvis kvinder havde adgang til frivillig familieplanlægning. Universel adgang til frivillig familieplanlægning er en omfattende og kostnadseffektiv løsning for at opnå alle FN's mål for udvikling. Udover at reducere moderdødelighed, hjælper det unge kvinder med at undgå tidlige graviditeter, gør det muligt for flere piger at blive i skolen længere, giver kvinder mulighed for at få færre, sundere børn og bryder den intergenerationelle kæde af fattigdom. Det reducerer også HIV-overførsel, styrker kvinder i deres evne til at drive indkomstskabende aktiviteter og fremmer miljømæssig bæredygtighed. Dette er også en god økonomisk investering. Internationale familieplanlægningsprogrammer leverer en af de højeste afkast på investeringen blandt alle udviklingsindsatser. Forskning fra Guttmacher-instituttet viser, at at levere kvalitetsbaseret reproduktiv sundhedspleje og moderne præventionsmidler til alle kvinder, der ønsker og har brug for dem, reducerer omkostningerne til moder- og nyfødtomsorg — og resulterer i en nettobesparelse på 1,5 milliarder dollar for hver investeret dollar. Trods sin lave pris og store fordele har frivillig familieplanlægning ikke konsekvent modtaget tilstrækkelig finansiering fra verdensledere. Den nuværende økonomiske situation har tvunget Kongressen til at genvurdere udgiftsforholdene — og med rette. Men for ofte er behovene for kvinder og børn de første, der bliver afskåret. Dette års budgetforhandlinger var ingen undtagelse. To af de mest bekymrende og kortsigtede besparelser er de i finansieringen af internationale familieplanlægningsprogrammer og FN's Folkefonds (UNFPA). UNFPA er FN's agentur, der er dedikeret til at hjælpe regeringer med at levere omfattende seksuel og reproduktiv sundhedspleje — inklusive frivillig familieplanlægning — gennem kvinderes livscyklus verden over. En af de klogeste investeringer, jeg nogensinde har gjort, var min donation på 1 milliard dollar til FN, som bidrog til at etablere FN-Foundation. FN er den eneste institution med den globale rækkevidde og kapacitet til at tackle dagens største udfordringer. Hvis vi ønsker at efterlade vores børn og børnebørn en sikker og sund planet, skal verdensledere støtte FN's afgørende arbejde med frivillig familieplanlægning og reproduktiv sundhed for kvinder verden over. Tiden er nu. De investeringer, vi foretager i dag, vil definere den verden, vi overdrager til den næste generation. For at opretholde sin globale lederskabsrolle skal USA prioritere kloge, fremadrettede investeringer, der hjælper os med at håndtere både nuværende og fremtidige ansvar. Den bedste måde at gøre det på er at lytte til kvinder — og finansiere internationale familieplanlægningsprogrammer. Vores fremtid afhænger af det. Meningerne i denne kommentar er udelukkende de af Ted Turner.

article_content: Liverpool FC has taken a significant step toward expanding Anfield Stadium’s capacity from 44,000 to 54,000, after council planners recommended approving their proposal. Liverpool aims to eventually increase Anfield’s total capacity to 58,800 following the completion of this first phase. The club confirms that domestic and European home games will continue uninterrupted throughout the construction period. Anfield, which recently hosted a sold-out Premier League clash against Aston Villa attended by 44,689 fans, remains one of football’s most iconic venues.

article_content: Shadow Minister for Sport Clive Efford was among the first to condemn the Premier League for failing to invest adequately in grassroots football following the announcement of a £5 billion television rights deal. He stated, 'These are incredible sums of money — it would be nothing short of criminal if none of the extra revenue went to expanding participation at the grassroots level.' Yet, it was noted that on the very day after the TV deal was sealed, Efford attended the opening of a new £400,000 3G football pitch in his Eltham constituency — a project funded jointly by the Premier League and the Football Foundation. The Premier League reportedly requested that their name be included in Efford’s official statement acknowledging the project, but he declined, insisting his original wording stood on its own merits. Efford urged the league to live up to its pledge to dedicate 5% of domestic TV income to grassroots development. The Premier League countered that, alongside solidarity payments, it already contributes more than this threshold. Efford remained unconvinced: 'If that were true, there’d be far more pitches and qualified coaches at the community level.' Meanwhile, the England Cricket Board has granted Eoin Morgan, captain of the ODI team, permission to compete in the full Indian Premier League (IPL), despite a scheduling clash with England’s domestic T20 season. Morgan, who has struggled for form in World Cup preparations, will benefit from high-level exposure ahead of the 2016 World Twenty20 in India — a rare concession granted by both the ECB and his county, Middlesex. In a rare display of warmth, Chelsea manager Jose Mourinho greeted Hollywood actor Willem Dafoe with a hearty hug and invited him into the dressing room. Mourinho, a BT Sport ambassador, reportedly met Dafoe during filming for the broadcaster. Chelsea, seeking a new shirt sponsor after a proposed deal with Turkish Airlines stalled, appointed former Liverpool CEO Christian Purslow to lead their commercial revival. Purslow has enlisted HTH Associates — founded by ex-Manchester United executives Leo Thompson and Harry Horsley — to assist in the search. However, past experience suggests such expertise doesn’t guarantee success: the FA’s attempt to hire former United sponsorship manager Phil Barker failed to attract a sponsor for the FA Cup this season. Bradford City’s Valley Parade pitch, in deplorable condition ahead of their FA Cup tie against Sunderland, suffered due to the limited budget of groundskeeper Mick Doyle, who resorted to a makeshift snowplough built from scrap wood. The club has now committed to relaying the pitch using proceeds from their cup run. Despite cutting around 15 staff, the ECB has invested in the marketing agency FutureProof to revamp fan engagement. Their first initiative, #LoveEngland, is seen as a modest improvement over the confusing #RISE campaign launched during the Ashes. Manchester United club secretary John Alexander was spotted in the Anfield directors’ box mouthing the lyrics to Liverpool’s anthem, 'You'll Never Walk Alone.' A former Spurs employee with deep Liverpool ties, Alexander has long been a source of amusement — and irritation — among United fans, even drawing ribbing from former manager Sir Alex Ferguson.

article_content: In the wake of a brutal tornado outbreak across the Midwest, where 76 storms left at least eight people dead and countless homes destroyed, one small ray of hope emerged. Spc. Jacob Montgomery, a five-year veteran of the Illinois Army National Guard, watched his apartment in Washington, Illinois, collapse into debris on November 17. Among his losses, nothing weighed heavier than the disappearance of his beloved pitbull, Dexter. Despite years of emergency training, Montgomery admitted he wasn’t prepared for the heartbreak of losing his dog. For days, he combed through the ruins, hoping against hope. Then came a miracle: a neighbor called with news that a local rescue team had found Dexter buried under rubble — lured out with hot dogs. 'All my stuff is gone,' Montgomery said, 'but Dexter? He was everything.' Now staying with a friend, he’s rebuilding his life — and finally, he’s not alone.

I flere dage gennemsøgte han ruinernes, med håb om et mirakel. article_content: Leicester City’s Director of Football, Terry Robinson, has been dismissed following the club’s alarming decline in the Premier League table. Robinson was informed of the decision by Chief Executive Susan Whelan after the Foxes went 11 games without a win. Leicester now sit at the bottom of the Barclays Premier League, having lost eight of their last nine matches — a run that has cost Robinson his position. Robinson, formerly chairman of Sheffield United, was also under scrutiny for an alleged racist remark made earlier this year. Reports claimed he referred to a club employee as a 'darkie' during a training ground conversation. Although the incident raised concerns among staff and prompted the FA and Leicester City to launch separate investigations, neither found sufficient evidence to pursue disciplinary action, as no formal complaints were filed. Sportsmail understands that Robinson’s dismissal is based purely on footballing grounds — specifically, inadequate player recruitment during the summer transfer window — and is unrelated to the earlier allegations. Manager Nigel Pearson’s position remains secure, according to club sources. In a club statement, Leicester confirmed Robinson’s immediate departure and announced that Academy Director Jon Rudkin — who has been with the club since 2003 and led the Academy to Elite Player Performance Plan (EPPP) Category One status — will assume the role of Director of Football. The club expressed gratitude for Robinson’s service and wished him well for the future.

article_content: A unique manuscript bearing Thomas Hardy’s only known attempt at composing a song is to be sold at auction. The faded document features lyrics and a melody, handwritten in pencil by the author of classic novels including Jude the Obscure and Far From the Madding Crowd. Written in 1922, the manuscript is expected to fetch at least £6,000 when auctioned by Bonhams in London. While several composers have set Hardy’s poems to music, this is the first known instance of Hardy himself creating both lyrics and melody. The song, titled 'O I Won't Lead a Homely Life,' includes a sixteen-bar D major melody written beneath the lyrics. The tune is believed to be derived from a traditional air Hardy recalled from his youth, possibly from his time singing in the choir at Stinsford Church near Dorchester. Hardy noted alternative lyrics for the final line — 'And sunk and sad was she' — to be used if the song were performed by a woman. Above the original line, he scribbled in red ink: 'And sad was life for me,' with a note: 'If sung by a woman, the words in red may be used.' The manuscript, the only surviving Hardy document combining his handwriting with original music, was once owned by Sydney Cockerell, Hardy’s literary executor after his death in 1928. Roy Davids, a 70-year-old manuscript dealer from Great Haseley near Oxford, is selling the piece. He explains that Hardy marked the manuscript 'To an old air,' indicating he adapted an existing melody rather than composing one from scratch. Hardy, raised in a musical family in Dorset, learned violin from his father and grandfather, and retained a remarkable memory for folk tunes. He continued playing throughout his life, even after becoming a celebrated author. Though Hardy published his first poetry collection, Wessex Poems, in 1898, he was not widely recognized as a major poet until the 1950s. Mike Nixon, Secretary of the Hardy Society, called the manuscript 'genuine' and 'extremely rare,' noting it was written on the reverse of a circular dated 23 August 1922. Born in 1840 in Stinsford, Dorset, Hardy was the son of a stonemason and a well-read mother who educated him until age eight. His formal schooling ended at 16 when he became an architect’s apprentice. After moving to London in 1862 and briefly studying at King’s College, he returned to Dorset in 1867 to focus on writing. The success of Far From the Madding Crowd (1874) allowed him to abandon architecture for literature, producing masterpieces like The Mayor of Casterbridge, Tess of the d’Urbervilles, and Jude the Obscure. Controversial themes in Tess and Jude — particularly their sympathetic portrayals of women and explicit sexual references — provoked public outrage. Some booksellers even wrapped copies in brown paper. Disillusioned, Hardy ceased writing fiction entirely in the early 1900s.
translated_content: Et unikt manuskript med Thomas Hardys eneste kendte forsøg på at skrive en sang skal sælges på auktion. Det forblegede dokument indeholder tekster og en melodi, håndskrevet i blyant af forfatteren bag klassiske værker som 'Jude den forfulgte' og 'Langt fra det trætte kvæg'. Skrivet i 1922, forventes manuskriptet at bringe mindst 6.000 britiske pund, når det går under hammeren hos Bonhams i London. Selv om flere komponister har sat Hardys digte til musik, er dette det første kendte eksempel på, at Hardy selv skabte både tekst og melodi. Sangen, med titlen 'O jeg vil ikke føre et hjemmeligt liv,' indeholder en seksten-noters D-dur-melodi, skrevet under teksten. Melodien antages at være baseret på en gammel vis, som Hardy huskede fra sin barndom, muligvis fra hans tid i koret i Stinsford Kirke nær Dorchester. Hardy noterede alternative vers til den sidste linje — 'og sank og trist var hun' — hvis sangen skulle synges af en kvinde. Over den oprindelige linje skrev han i rød blæk: 'og trist var livet for mig,' med en note: 'Hvis sangen synges af en kvinde, kan de røde ord bruges.' Manuskriptet, det eneste bevarede Hardy-manuskript, der kombinerer hans håndskrift med egen musik, tilhørte tidligere Sydney Cockerell, Hardys litterære eksekutor efter hans død i 1928. Roy Davids, en 70-årig manuskripthandler fra Great Haseley nær Oxford, sælger stykket. Han forklarer, at Hardy markerede manuskriptet med 'Til en gammel melodi,' hvilket indikerer, at han tilpassede en eksisterende melodi snarere end at skabe en ny. Hardy, opvokset i en musikalsk familie i Dorset, lærte at spille violin af sin far og bedstefar og beholdt en bemærkelsesværdig hukommelse for folketoner. Han fortsatte med at spille hele sit liv, selv efter at blive en berømt forfatter. Selv om Hardy udgav sin første digtsamling, 'Wessex Poems', i 1898, blev han ikke bredt anerkendt som en stor digter før 1950'erne. Mike Nixon, sekretær i Hardy-selskabet, kaldte manuskriptet 'autentisk' og 'yderst sjældent' og bemærkede, at det var skrevet på bagsiden af en cirkular datreret 23. august 1922. Født i 1840 i Stinsford, Dorset, var Hardy søn af en stenhugger og en vel læst mor, der underviste ham indtil han var otte år gammel. Hans formelle uddannelse sluttede ved 16, da han blev lærling hos en lokal arkitekt. Efter at have flyttet til London i 1862 og kortvarigt studeret ved Kings College, vendte han tilbage til sin elskede Dorset i 1867 for at konsentrere sig om skrivning. Succesen med 'Far From the Madding Crowd' (1874) gjorde det muligt for ham at opgive arkitektur og fokusere på en litterær karriere, som førte til værker som 'The Mayor of Casterbridge', 'Tess of the d'Urbervilles' og 'Jude the Obscure'. Kontroversielle temaer i 'Tess' og 'Jude' — især deres sympatiske fremstilling af kvinder og eksplikte seksuelle henvisninger — udløste offentlig vrede. Nogle boghandlere pakkerede kopier i brune papposer. Fortvivlet stoppede Hardy helt med at skrive romaner i begyndelsen af 1900-tallet.

article_content: Auditors have issued a scathing assessment of Iain Duncan Smith’s flagship welfare reform, Universal Credit, warning that its disastrous early rollout risks further taxpayer losses and should be delayed. The Work and Pensions Secretary blamed inept civil servants for the project’s failures, saying he had 'lost faith' in their ability to manage the £2.4 billion initiative. According to a damning report by the National Audit Office (NAO), Universal Credit suffers from weak management, ineffective controls, and poor governance. Designed to simplify welfare by replacing multiple out-of-work benefits and incentivizing work, the program has failed to deliver value for money—partly due to unrealistic deadlines set by ministers. A £425 million IT system remains dysfunctional, and £34 million worth of equipment has already been written off. While the NAO still sees potential for significant societal benefit, it urges the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) to scale back its ambitions and establish realistic timelines, potentially pushing the full rollout beyond 2017. Duncan Smith claimed he could have written the report himself, accusing officials of cultivating a 'fortress mentality' and a 'good news' culture that concealed problems. He said external experts from the Cabinet Office were brought in to regain control and stay within budget. Labour has demanded Duncan Smith appear before Parliament to explain why he repeatedly assured MPs the project was on track despite internal warnings. The NAO criticized the DWP for lacking a clear blueprint for the program and for failing to assess the value of over £300 million in developed systems. The report also noted the IT system lacks a crucial fraud-detection feature. Labour’s Liam Byrne condemned Duncan Smith for claiming the reform was sound while losing control of his department—at a cost of hundreds of millions. The DWP responded by pointing to improvements since April, when a former Olympics chief was appointed to 'reset' the project.

Et 425 mio. pund stort IT-system er stadig funktionelt utilstrækkeligt, og 34 mio. pund i udstyr er allerede afskrevet. Selv om NAO stadig ser potentiale for betydelige samfundsmæssige fordele, opfordrer den Det danske Arbejds- og Pensionsdepartement (DWP) til at skære ned på dets ambitioner og etablere realistiske tidsplaner, hvilket sandsynligvis vil forskyde fuld gennemførelse ud over 2017. article_content: By Suzannah Hills. PUBLISHED: 05:33 EST, 16 June 2013. | UPDATED: 01:51 EST, 17 June 2013. Iran is preparing to deploy 4,000 troops into Syria to support President Bashar al-Assad, following the U.S. announcement that it will provide military aid to Syrian rebels. President Barack Obama made the pledge earlier this week after the U.S. claimed to have found conclusive evidence that Assad’s regime had used chemical weapons against rebel forces — including hardline Sunni Islamists — and urged Britain and France to join the effort. While Britain has not yet committed to arming the rebels, over 350 Royal Marines have been deployed to Jordan as part of an 8,000-strong multinational exercise, further heightening tensions in the war-torn region. A video posted on YouTube shows a Syrian rebel using a shoulder-fired, heat-seeking SA-16 missile — a Soviet-era weapon capable of targeting aircraft up to 11,000 feet — raising concerns about how well-armed rebel groups already are. The footage has intensified fears that arming moderate rebels could result in advanced weapons falling into the hands of anti-Western extremists. Sources suggest the 12-day exercise, named Eager Lion, is designed to position NATO forces for potential humanitarian operations in Syria. As the West debates whether to intervene militarily — with over 100,000 people killed in two years — the regional conflict has deepened into a sectarian divide between Sunni and Shia Muslims. According to The Independent, Iran’s decision to send troops predates its presidential election earlier this week. The sectarian rift stems from longstanding theological disagreements: Sunnis believe Abu Bakr, the father-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, was his rightful successor, while Shiites revere Ali, his son-in-law. The U.S. now aligns with wealthy Sunni-majority Gulf states — from Egypt and Turkey to Jordan — while Iran and predominantly Shia Iraq, which the West helped liberate from Saddam Hussein’s Sunni minority rule, back Assad. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin has openly opposed Western efforts to arm Syrian rebels. In response to the EU’s lifting of its arms embargo, Putin reaffirmed Russia’s intent to supply Assad with advanced anti-aircraft systems to deter foreign intervention. Following the U.S. announcement, Assad claimed on Lebanese television that Syria had received its first shipment of Russia’s S-300 air defense system. Prime Minister David Cameron is scheduled to meet Putin amid fears that diverging positions are pushing the West and Russia toward a new Cold War. Cameron has pledged to hold a parliamentary vote if Britain decides to arm the rebels, under pressure from Conservative backbenchers. He welcomed Obama’s move but has not yet committed to sending weapons, emphasizing continued non-lethal support for what he calls the 'genuine' opposition — those seeking a democratic, pluralistic Syria that protects minorities, including Christians. 'Yes, there are deeply unsavoury elements within the Syrian opposition — dangerous, extremist, linked to al-Qaida — and I want nothing to do with them,' Cameron told Sky News’s Murnaghan programme. 'But there are others who want a free, democratic Syria. We must work with them. If we don’t, the only ones gaining ground will be those we condemn.' Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg took a cautious stance, telling the BBC’s Andrew Marr programme that arming rebels at this stage is 'not the right thing to do.' He stressed the need to avoid entangling Britain in a civil war with no clear military solution. Former Liberal Democrat leader Lord Ashdown warned that Western involvement risks being manipulated into a broader Sunni-Shia proxy war. 'This isn't about Syria — it’s the front line in a far wider struggle,' he said. 'We’re being used to support Sunnis while Russia backs Shiites. That’s folly.' Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi announced the severing of diplomatic ties with Syria and closure of its embassy in Cairo, responding to pressure from hardline Sunni clerics calling for a 'holy war' against Assad. Parliamentary opposition to arming rebels remains strong across all major UK parties, and international consensus remains fractured as the G8 prepares to address the crisis.
